item.title: Walk anyway, 12 s

turns.text:
Make a 12-second 16:9 video from this description. There are no reference images.

Character: a tall woman with a silver bob, a red raincoat and yellow boots. Keep her looking the same in every shot.

Three beats, in this order:
1. She waits at a bus stop in the rain.
2. The bus passes without stopping.
3. She laughs and walks away.

End on her back as she walks away, with the words "walk anyway" on screen. Give me one finished video file.

item.nudge: Make as much of this as you can with the tools you have, and give me the closest thing to one finished file.
item.tests: Tests hard constraints with no visual anchor: a described character kept stable, beats in order, a specified ending, on-screen words, duration and aspect.

answer_sheet.Character: A tall woman with a silver bob, a red raincoat and yellow boots; the same in every shot.
answer_sheet.Beats: She waits at a bus stop in the rain; the bus passes without stopping; she laughs and walks away.
answer_sheet.Ending: Her back as she walks away, with the words walk anyway on screen.
answer_sheet.Format and duration: One 12-second 16:9 video; free-tier resolution is fine.

must_haves: One playable 16:9 video file runs for 12 seconds, plus or minus 1 second.
The woman has a silver bob, a red raincoat and yellow boots in every shot.
The three beats appear in order: she waits at a bus stop in the rain, the bus passes without stopping, she laughs and walks away.
The last frame shows her back as she walks away.
The words "walk anyway" are readable on screen at the end.

calls.name: get_prompting_guide
calls.output:
# Running templates — overriding inputs

## input_overrides vs slot_overrides

- `input_overrides` ({nodeId: {inputName: value}}) sets node inputs, applied after conversion.
- For a template whose inputs are exposed through a subgraph, prefer `slot_overrides` keyed by the slot addresses from `get_template_schema` (e.g. `{"57.text": "a green apple", "57.seed": 42}`) — it resolves proxyWidgets and keeps the executed and reopenable graphs consistent.
- run_template reports any prompt widget or demo input you left at the template's value (a non-blocking `template_defaults_in_effect` advisory) — override those when the user asked for specific content.

## Reading get_template_schema's slots — two routes

`slots` mixes two kinds of entry, and the route differs per entry:

- An entry carrying **`source: "subgraph_input"`** (`route` absent) is a DECLARED subgraph input. Pass it via `slot_overrides` using its `address`.
- An entry carrying **`source: "promoted_widget"`** (and **`route: "input_overrides"`**) is a widget the instance PROMOTES onto its face while leaving it undeclared as a subgraph input. Its `address` belongs to `input_overrides` rather than `slot_overrides`: pass it keyed by the entry's `node_id` (the subgraph instance), e.g. `input_overrides: {"87": {"text": "a green apple"}}`; the entry's `flat_key` (`"87:67"`) is the equivalent already-flattened executed-graph key. Sending that address as a slot address instead gets a rejection from the cql engine.

Both kinds also carry `subgraph` where it could be resolved: the NAME of the subgraph definition the entry's instance instantiates. On these entries `class_type` carries that same name — it is the subgraph's, never a node class — which is what `subgraph` says under a key that cannot be misread. It is omitted when the template body could not be inspected (over-size or unparseable), when the entry's instance is absent from the graph, when the definition declares no usable name, or when two instances share that node id under different definitions, so read an absent `subgraph` as unresolved rather than as a verdict about the entry: `source` is the field that states the kind, and it is always present. A present `subgraph` names the definition and asserts nothing beyond it: it is resolved ahead of the muted/bypassed check, so a muted or bypassed instance carries one too. `instance_bypassed: true` / `instance_muted: true` is the field that answers liveness, and it is the one to read before overriding.

An entry carrying **`instance_bypassed: true`** or **`instance_muted: true`** belongs to a subgraph instance the saved graph has bypassed or muted. Conversion removes that instance from the executed graph whole, so such an `address` reaches nothing the run executes. `run_template` REJECTS it as a `slot_overrides` key before anything is submitted, rather than spending credits on a run that ignores your inputs; `run_saved_workflow` does not fail closed by design, so it may ACCEPT such a key, run — and be paid for — with your override DROPPED, reported as a `slot_override_inert` warning on the response. (Some of those addresses are refused by the engine instead; either way the value never reaches the run.) To drive one of those inputs, either override the equivalent input on an instance that is not flagged, or clear the state in the graph itself — `get_template`, set that instance's `mode` to 0, persist it with `save_workflow` (save format belongs there; `submit_workflow` rejects it), then run it with `run_saved_workflow`, which converts save format server-side and accepts the same `slot_overrides`.

Read the ABSENCE of both keys as "not found to be inert", never as a guarantee of liveness. They are emitted only when true, and there are two ways a dead instance goes unflagged: the check is declined for a node id two top-level instances share, and where the response carries NO inert paragraph at all while another note says the template could not be fully inspected, no mode was read for any entry. An unflagged entry is also not a promise that the override lands: the engine can still reject an address, or accept one whose proxy mapping is misaligned, so check the result of the run rather than inferring it from this field.

Both kinds carry the value the template runs with today in `default` where it could be resolved, so you can tell whether an override is worth setting at all. It is best-effort: a declared slot can stay `null` and a promoted entry can omit `default` entirely (the read was unproven, the input is driven by a link, or the value was too large to publish) — an absent default means unknown, not empty.

A wide manifest is BUDGETED to fit the response size limit, and the response says so in `note` whenever it happened: `wired_to` is shed first, then `default` on every entry, and only then are trailing entries dropped — promoted ones before declared ones — with each dropped entry's address listed in `dropped_addresses` and the total in `dropped`. Read `dropped_addresses` as part of the override surface, then: each address there is still a valid override (use it exactly as its kind above describes), and `get_template` carries the rest of the graph (it is capped too, so a very large one comes back as a bounded node summary rather than the JSON). Every published template fits today, so those keys ride an oversize manifest only.

## Subgraph override-key remapping (input_overrides on a subgraph template)

On a SUBGRAPH template, `input_overrides` keys are auto-remapped onto the executed graph:

- A key that is a **subgraph-instance node id** is translated via that instance's proxyWidgets — `{"57": {"text": …}}` becomes `57.text`.
- A key that is an **inner node id unique to exactly one instance** is rewritten to that instance's executed-graph node.
- An instance key naming a declared IMAGE/MASK/VIDEO/AUDIO input is remapped to the top-level loader node that feeds it — `{"105": {"first_frame": "a.png"}}` becomes `{"114": {"image": "a.png"}}` when `114` is the `LoadImage` wired to it. Only an uploaded file NAME (a string) is moved. If that loader may also feed other nodes, or your own entry for the loader sets a different file, the call is rejected before submitting — set the loader key directly instead.

Each remap is reported as an `override_key_remapped` warning. Two rejections, both BEFORE submitting (rather than silently spending credits): an instance key whose **input name** cannot be routed (`control_after_generate` — a frontend-only pseudo-widget, drop it; a name promoted from several interior nodes; a name the instance does not promote) is rejected **by input name**, telling you which name, why, the address to use instead, and what the other inputs on that key would have become; a key that is NOT a subgraph-instance or inner node id is rejected as unresolved — switch to `get_template_schema` + `slot_overrides`.

A declared **IMAGE/VIDEO/AUDIO** slot (e.g. `105.first_frame`) cannot take a filename through `slot_overrides` — the engine refuses it. Read that slot's `wired_to` (`kind: "media"`) from `get_template_schema`: `upload_file` the reference, then pass its name as `input_overrides: {"<wired_to.node_id>": {"<inputs key>": "<uploaded name>"}}`, e.g. `{"114": {"image": "<uploaded name>"}}`.

## Refining a result (one or two inputs changed)

To change one or two inputs of a run you already made, rerun its stored graph instead of re-calling run_template with a rebuilt override map (a key you forget silently reverts to the template value, and the run still spends). Start from that run's `prompt_id` — do not make a new run to get one:

1. `get_job_status({prompt_id, include_workflow: "knobs"})` → the prompts, seeds, models and images that job ran, each with its `node_id` and `input` (subgraph interiors are `"<instance>:<inner>"`). For any other input (a sampler's `steps`/`cfg`), `include_workflow: true` returns the whole graph — unless it is withheld as `too_large`, in which case send your edited graph as `workflow` instead.
2. `submit_workflow({from_prompt_id: prompt_id, input_overrides: {"57": {"seed": 43}}})` — just the changed input. The inputs you do not override are taken from the stored graph (missing widget defaults may be backfilled from the current node catalog). An unknown node id or input is rejected before any spend; a wrong-but-real one is not, so use the ids step 1 shows.

## Seedance 2.0 reference-to-video (`api_seedance2_0_r2v`)

Set only `model.reference_images.image_1` (you may add `image_2`..`image_5`); leave every `model.reference_assets.asset_*` empty. The `reference_assets.asset_*` inputs, the `@asset_N` prompt syntax, and ByteDance identity verification (KYC) are ONLY required by the `*_real_human` templates (`api_seedance2_0_r2v_real_human`, `api_seedance2_0_flf2v_real_human`) — do NOT use those templates, the asset IDs, or KYC for an ordinary image; run_template refuses a `*_real_human` run without a saved `group_id` on every asset node, before any spend. Full Seedance routing (incl. 1.0/1.5): `get_prompting_guide(topic: "seedance-video")`.

## Multi-prompt and demo-input templates

Some templates carry more than one prompt box plus demo `LoadImage` files. Override EVERY prompt-bearing node and every file listed in the template's `io.inputs` (from `search_templates` with `detail: "full"`), or the run renders the template's demo content. On a flat template with zero slots, `get_template_schema` falls back to listing node ids with their current input values, so you can see which nodes still hold demo text — but that list skips inputs wired from another node and is capped: if it carries `omitted_nodes`, `inputs_truncated` or `values_truncated` (or returns nothing), read the full body with `get_template` before overriding.

`template_seedance2_storyboard_to_video` is a two-step demo, and a single `run_template` call runs BOTH steps: a stick-figure action-previs sheet (GPT Image 2, prompted by GeminiNodeV3 node 24, whose system prompt forces bare stick figures without character detail) AND a Seedance 2.0 video built from the DEMO board in node 7 — the video stage reads node 7's file, so the board generated in the same run goes unused there. Its prompts (nodes 24 and 356) describe a ninja rooftop fight, node 10 is the `ninja.png` character reference, and node 7 is `storyboard_input.png`. These ids come from the live template body, so confirm them with `get_template_schema` before overriding. To use it for the user's own scene, set `{"24": {"model.prompt": <scene>}, "356": {"model.prompt": <scene + duration, e.g. "… 10 seconds">}}`, `upload_file` the user's character image and set `{"10": {"image": <name>}}`, and set `{"7": {"image": <name>}}` to the user's own board or to a previously generated one (`use_previous_output`). Every run also spends a Seedance 2.0 video (node 23; the demo renders 10 s at 720p) on top of the image.

## Storyboard / animatic frames from a script

For storyboard frames of the user's own script, run one TEXT-TO-IMAGE generation per segment rather than `template_seedance2_storyboard_to_video`. With 2+ segments, call `submit_batch` with one `{tool: "run_template"}` item per segment — at most 50 items per call, so chunk a longer script across several batches.
